title: Stereo geometry
description: Already rectified data (KITTI P_rect, Middlebury, ETH3D) needs no remapping:
html:
fastforks.stereo.geometry turns a calibrated camera pair into the rectified image pair a stereo model expects, and its disparity back into depth and point clouds. It needs numpy and torch only; OpenCV is used only as a test oracle.

from fastforks.stereo import geometry as g

rig = g.read_calib("calib_cam_to_cam.txt", "kitti-unrectified")  # a StereoRig
rect = g.rectify(rig)  # rotations, rectified intrinsics, Q; no maps yet
left_r, right_r = rect.remap(left, right)  # builds the maps once (per device), then reuses them
disparity = ...  # any fastforks stereo model on (left_r, right_r)
depth = rect.depth(disparity)  # metres, rectified left view
cloud = rect.point_cloud(disparity, colors=left_r, frame="camera")  # cloud.points, cloud.colors
depth_left = rect.unrectify(depth)  # depth in the original left image

Already rectified data (KITTI P_rect, Middlebury, ETH3D) needs no remapping:

rig = g.read_calib("calib.txt")  # Middlebury: a RectifiedRig(f, baseline, cx, cy, doffs)
cloud = rig.point_cloud(disparity, colors=left)
rig = g.RectifiedRig(f=721.5, cx=609.6, cy=172.9, baseline=0.54)  # or by hand

With doffs > 0 (Middlebury), points farther than f * baseline / doffs need a negative disparity, which the networks do not predict: their depth is plausible but wrong. Rectify a StereoRig instead (rectify gives both images one principal point, doffs = 0).

End-to-end example

A raw (unrectified) KITTI pair and its calib_cam_to_cam.txt to a coloured point cloud in the original left camera frame and a depth map at the raw left image's pixels. The images stay on the model's device from the remap to the cloud; tests/test_geometry_example.py runs this block on rendered images with a stand-in model. calib_cam_to_cam.txt is KITTI raw's calibration file; the images must have its S_xx size (else InputError names both sizes).

import numpy as np
import torch
from PIL import Image

from fastforks import stereo
from fastforks.stereo import geometry as g

model = stereo.load("igev-stereo-sceneflow")  # on the GPU if there is one
rig = g.read_calib("calib_cam_to_cam.txt", "kitti-unrectified")  # both cameras with their distortion, R, T
rect = g.rectify(rig)  # rotations, rectified intrinsics, Q; the maps are built on first use


def raw(path):  # [3, H, W] uint8 on the model's device
    return torch.from_numpy(np.array(Image.open(path).convert("RGB"))).permute(2, 0, 1).to(model.device)


left_r, right_r = rect.remap(raw("left.png"), raw("right.png"))  # rectified on that device, maps cached there
disparity = model(left_r, right_r).disparity  # [H, W] pixels, rectified left view
cloud = rect.point_cloud(disparity, colors=left_r.permute(1, 2, 0), frame="camera")  # original left camera frame
points, colors = cloud.points[cloud.valid].cpu().numpy(), cloud.colors[cloud.valid].cpu().numpy()  # [N, 3] each
depth_left = rect.unrectify(rect.depth(disparity))  # [h, w] metres at the raw left pixels, NaN where unknown

Camera models

One frozen dataclass per model; all satisfy the Camera protocol (project(points) -> (pixels, valid), unproject(pixels) -> (rays, valid), numpy or torch in, the same type out, float64). g.camera(model_id, w, h, fx, fy, cx, cy, *coefficients) builds one from a model id and its coefficients in file order.

The E57 models are the image representations of ASTM E2807 (.e57 laser scans): pinhole images looking along -z with y down, and spherical (azimuth / elevation) and cylindrical panoramas around +z. They project and unproject like the others (e.g. to colour a scan or turn a panorama into rays), but rectify rejects them. Reading .e57 files themselves (a binary point cloud container) is out of scope.

The tests compare with reference values from a Rust implementation (tools/geometry_goldens/ff_goldens.rs, regeneration steps in its header), stored in tests/data/geometry_goldens.json, so the tests need no Rust toolchain. pinhole-opencv marks rays past the distortion fold (where the radial polynomial turns back, e.g. 44 degrees off axis for k1 = -0.35) invalid in both directions, so they cannot alias pixels nearer the centre; OpenCV and the Rust reference return them.

Rectification

rectify(rig, *, size=None, focal=None, alpha=None, fov_max=120.0) works the same way for every camera model:

  • R1, R2 follow Bouguet's method (as cv2.stereoRectify): each camera is rotated half way, then both onto the baseline.
  • K_new is one focal length and principal point for both views. Default: the left camera's fx at the rectified size and the image centre, the same as model(left, right, rig=rig); focal= sets the focal length. alpha= instead picks K_new as OpenCV does (0: only valid pixels, 1: all source pixels) from unprojected samples of the image borders, as are the valid-pixel rectangles roi_left / roi_right.
  • Each rectified pixel p maps to the source pixel cam.project(R_i^T K_new^-1 p).
  • Wide-angle and fisheye images are rectified onto a plane. Border rays beyond fov_max (full angle, degrees, < 180) are clamped to it, so a 200 degree lens gives a finite image of the central fov_max degrees.
  • Vertical rigs and swapped cameras raise InputError.

Rectification holds R1 R2 P1 P2 Q roi_left roi_right (OpenCV conventions) and builds the maps lazily per device. maps(device) returns them as [2, H, W, 2] source pixel coordinates (-1 where invalid) plus the valid mask. remap(left, right, *, device=None, return_valid=False) warps both images in one grid_sample call. It accepts HW, HWC or BHWC numpy and HW, CHW or BCHW torch, keeps the dtype (integers rounded) and fills invalid pixels with 0. depth and point_cloud mark rectified pixels without a source pixel (the black border with alpha > 0) invalid, so disparities a network predicts there do not end up in the cloud; unrectify ignores them too.

Agreement with OpenCV

whattolerance
R1, R2 vs cv2.stereoRectify / cv2.fisheye.stereoRectify1e-12
P1, P2, Q, mild distortion (k1 = -0.04)1e-6 px
P1, P2, Q, strong distortion (k1 = -0.28), alpha 0 / 0.5 / 10.05 / 0.25 / 0.4 px
maps vs cv2.initUndistortRectifyMap with the same R, P1e-3 px
remap uint8 / uint16 vs cv2.remap INTER_LINEAR1 LSB

The gap for strong distortion comes from OpenCV: stereoRectify undistorts the border points with only 5 fixed-point iterations, which have not converged at k1 = -0.28. fastforks iterates to convergence; the rectified images differ by at most a fraction of a pixel in scale. cv2.fisheye.stereoRectify picks K_new with its own balance rule, so only the rotations and the maps (given our P) are compared there.

Speed and memory

Both images of a pair, RGB uint8, strong distortion, alpha 0; RTX 5060 Ti, Ryzen 7 5800X with 4 threads, median of 10 (CPU) / 20 (GPU) runs (tools/bench_geometry.py):

sizeOpenCV CPU remaptorch CPU remaptorch GPU remap (tensors on GPU / numpy in and out)GPU peak allocated
720x12801.9 ms29 ms0.39 / 1.6 ms71 MB
1080x19206.3 ms64 ms1.1 / 6.3 ms156 MB
3000x400036 ms428 ms8.1 / 45 ms894 MB

The first remap on a device also builds the maps (float32, every camera model): 86 / 165 / 819 ms on the CPU, against 3 / 7 / 50 ms for cv2.initUndistortRectifyMap, and 0.24-0.32 s on the GPU, of which all but 9 / 14 / 65 ms is CUDA loading its kernels on first use (a second rectification on a warm GPU builds in that time). The first unrectify builds its inverse map with the iterative undistortion: 0.2-0.4 s on the GPU, 0.6 / 1.5 / 7.4 s on the CPU. Without a GPU and with OpenCV installed, cv2.remap with the maps from rect.maps() is about 10x faster than the torch CPU path.

Calibration files

read_calib(path, format=None, cameras=None, size=None, unit=None, right=None, names=None) detects the format from the content:

Results are in metres. KITTI baselines use the exact t_x = (P[0, 3] - cx P[2, 3]) / f of each projection (the P[0, 3] difference alone is 0.2 % short on odometry sequence 00). Kalibr cameras=(1, 0) reads cam1 as the left camera. KITTI files without camera 2 (KITTI-360 perspective.txt) default to cameras=(0, 1). ZED files hold every resolution (2K, FHD, FHD1200, HD, SVGA, VGA); the rotation is Rodrigues(RX, CV, RZ) of the chosen resolution and the translation (-Baseline, TY, TZ) in mm, as in Stereolabs' OpenCV samples. Rotations must be orthonormal to 1e-4 (files round to about 1e-6); they are snapped to the nearest exact rotation. YAML is read with a small built-in parser (no PyYAML); anchors, aliases and flow mappings raise InputError. DSO camera.txt (one camera, no pair) is not a stereo format. The OAK and RealSense readers are not verified on a device: the vendors' extrinsics direction ("from" and "to") differs between SDK versions, so a file that puts the right camera on the left of the left one (T_x > 0, swapped cameras) raises InputError with the fix; a baseline outside 5 mm to 1 m warns about a wrong unit=. COLMAP translations are in the model's arbitrary units; unit= takes a number, the factor to metres. RealSense inverse_brown_conrady is only accepted with zero coefficients.

The Gen1 Aria SLAM cameras sit sideways and face away from each other (rectify rejects that pair as vertical); Gen2's front pair is a usable horizontal one.

Any camera profile with intrinsics and poses

For a dataset without a read_calib format, build the two cameras and pass their camera-to-world poses to StereoRig.from_poses (keyword-only poses: world frame and unit are written at the call). axes="opencv" (x right, y down, z forward) is the default, "opengl" is nerfstudio / Blender; unit is the unit of the translations ("m", "cm", "mm" or a number, the factor to metres); non-rigid matrices (scale, shear, a projection) raise InputError. SHOW3D (poses in mm; headset0 / headset1 are a 64 mm stereo pair, frame 0 of a sample scene):

import json, numpy as np
from PIL import Image
from fastforks import stereo
from fastforks.stereo import geometry as g


def show3d(name, frame=0):  # camera + 4x4 T_WorldFromCamera of camera_calibration/<name>.json
    c = json.load(open(f"camera_calibration/{name}.json"))
    t = c["T_WorldFromCamera_by_index"][str(frame)] if "T_WorldFromCamera_by_index" in c else c
    return g.camera("pinhole", c["ImageSizeX"], c["ImageSizeY"], c["fx"], c["fy"], c["cx"], c["cy"]), t[
        "T_WorldFromCamera"
    ]


(left, pose_l), (right, pose_r) = show3d("headset0"), show3d("headset1")
rig = g.StereoRig.from_poses(
    left, right, left_to_world=pose_l, right_to_world=pose_r, unit="mm"
)  # rig.baseline 0.064 m
rect = g.rectify(rig, focal=450)  # the rectified focal length is yours to choose
left_r, right_r = rect.remap(np.array(Image.open("headset0_0.png")), np.array(Image.open("headset1_0.png")))
depth = rect.depth(stereo.load("las2-s")(left_r, right_r).disparity)  # metres, rectified left view

The left camera is the one whose right neighbour sits on its +x side; the other order raises in rectify ("swap the two cameras"). Pose lists are not read for you: pass the matrices of the frame you want.

Points from depth / points are in the left camera's frame; to world coordinates use p @ R.T + t with the rotation R and translation t of left_to_world.

Rigs with many cameras

A calibration file with many cameras (COLMAP, Kalibr, Aria, nerfstudio) gives one pair per call: pick it with read_calib(path, names=("cam_a", "cam_b")) (or cameras=(i, j) by index). Load the model once and loop:

model = stereo.load("las2-s")
for a, b in [("cam0", "cam1"), ("cam1", "cam2")]:
    rig = g.read_calib("rig.yaml", names=(a, b))
    result = model(left_image[a], right_image[b], rig=rig)

Keep the unit in mind: COLMAP and nerfstudio poses are in scene units, so depth is too, until you pass unit= (a number, the factor to metres). Pinhole pairs turned more than about 20 degrees against each other, or a size far above the model's training size, can give disparities beyond the model's range (about 176 px for las2-s) and wrong depth; rectify warns ("poor rectification") when such a turn is large (fisheye and 360 inputs are not limited by the turn) or when less than 10 % of the rectified image is valid.

Out of scope: calibrating a rig from checkerboard images, and rectification without calibration.

Rectified size and focal length

Sizes are (height, width) everywhere, the order of tensor shapes (calibration files keep their own order and are converted on read). A size that swaps portrait and landscape against the images or the calibration raises InputError. rectify(rig, size=..., focal=...): the rectified size defaults to the image size and the focal length to the left camera's fx (focal= and alpha= exclude each other); a RectifiedRig without cx, cy takes the image centre ((W - 1) / 2, (H - 1) / 2). rig.resized((h, w)) rescales a calibration to other images with c' = (c + 0.5) s - 0.5. A calibrated call does this for images of another size only if the aspect ratio stays (one pixel of rounding): a change of aspect ratio (crops or pads) raises InputError (shift cx, cy for crops; pass rig.resized(...) for an anisotropic resize on purpose). A size change that keeps the aspect ratio is assumed to be a resize of the whole view, and logs one warning per (calibration, size); a same-aspect crop cannot be told from it by the image alone, so give such images a calibration of the cropped size (cx, cy shifted by the crop offset), and a RectifiedRig with a size is rescaled the same way (other aspect ratios raise InputError). rect.depth(..., view="right"), rect.point_cloud(..., view="right") and rect.unrectify(..., view="right") use the right camera's rotation and maps; holes are NaN.

Calibrated calls keep the rectification maps of the last 8 (calibration, image size, size, focal) combinations per model (FIFO; an older one is rebuilt when used again). Each holds GPU maps of the rectified size, so many different rigs in one process cycle through that bound; the GPU memory that the allocator reserved for it stays reserved until torch.cuda.empty_cache().
